statement: Two similar triangles have areas of 9 and 25 square units. A side of the smaller one is 6 units. How long is the matching side of the larger one?

choices.misconception: I added the difference between the areas' square roots to the side rather than multiplying by their ratio.
I doubled the side because the larger area is roughly double the smaller.
I used the ratio of the areas as if it were the ratio of the lengths, then adjusted.
I multiplied the side by the ratio of the areas divided by three, mixing up which ratio applies to lengths.

hints: Areas scale by the square of the length factor.
If every length is multiplied by k then every area is multiplied by k squared. Work backwards from the area ratio to find k, and only then apply it to the side.
The area ratio is 25 to 9, so the length ratio is 5 to 3. Then 6 x 5 divided by 3 = 10.

solutions.reliable: Lengths scale by k and areas by k squared. Here the areas are in the ratio 25 to 9, so k squared is 25/9 and k is 5/3. Applying that to the side: 6 x 5/3 = 10. Check: the larger triangle's area should be (5/3) squared = 25/9 times the smaller, which it is. The transferable idea: take the square root of an area ratio before applying it to a length.
solutions.elegant: 9 and 25 are 3 squared and 5 squared, so the shapes are in the ratio 3 to 5 and the side goes 6 to 10.

whyOnTest: Applying an area ratio directly to a length is one of the highest-frequency errors on the whole paper, at every band.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
